problem.summary: The paper argues that mainstream detectors enumerate a nearly exhaustive set of candidate boxes and classify each, then clean up duplicates with IoU-based NMS: this is wasteful, inefficient, hard to train end-to-end, and depends on hand-tuned anchor assignment.
statements: Detectors must slide or enumerate a dense set of candidate boxes/anchors over the image and classify each one, wasting computation on background locations.
NMS post-processing is hard to differentiate and train, so most current detectors are not end-to-end trainable.
Anchor-based assignment needs manual foreground/background IoU thresholds and misses objects that no anchor covers sufficiently.

evidence.quote: Most successful object detectors enumerate a nearly exhaustive list of potential object locations and classify each. This is wasteful, inefficient, and requires additional post-processing.
This post-processing is hard to differentiate and train [23], hence most current detectors are not end-to-end trainable.
Sliding window based object detectors are however a bit wasteful, as they need to enumerate all possible object locations and dimensions.

background.summary: CenterNet builds on fully convolutional keypoint estimation (CornerNet, ExtremeNet, stacked hourglass) and on one-stage anchor detectors; the claimed gap is that prior keypoint detectors need a slow combinatorial grouping stage while anchor detectors need anchors, IoU thresholds and NMS.

relatedWork.quote: CornerNet [30] detects two bounding box corners as keypoints

relatedWork.quote: However, they require a combinatorial grouping stage after keypoint detection, which significantly slows down each algorithm.

evidence.quote: A center point can be seen as a single shape-agnostic anchor
Object detection is then a standard keypoint estimation problem [3,39,60].

solution.summary: CenterNet models each object as the center point of its bounding box, predicts a keypoint heatmap plus size/offset (and optional depth, orientation, pose) heads in one fully convolutional pass, and decodes boxes by extracting local heatmap peaks instead of NMS.
solution.approach: Detect objects as center points on a keypoint heatmap and regress their size and other attributes from image features at those points, with peak extraction replacing NMS.
components: Gaussian-rendered center keypoint heatmap trained with focal loss
local offset head to recover output-stride discretization error
object size regression head with L1 loss
peak extraction (8-connected neighbors, top-100) via 3x3 max pooling instead of NMS
optional 3D (depth, dimensions, orientation) and human pose heads

evidence.quote: We model an object as a single point — the center point of its bounding box.
Inference is a single network forward-pass, without non-maximal suppression for post-processing.
First, our CenterNet assigns the “anchor” based solely on location, not box overlap [18].
The peak keypoint extraction serves as a sufficient NMS alternative and can be implemented efficiently on device using a 3 × 3 max pooling operation.

experiments.summary: The authors evaluate on MS COCO (train2017/val2017/test-dev) with AP, AP50 and AP75 across four backbones and three test-augmentation levels, compare speed/accuracy against one- and two-stage detectors on a fixed machine, and additionally report KITTI 3D detection, COCO keypoint pose, Pascal VOC, plus ablations on resolution, loss weights and training schedule.

evidence.quote: CenterNet achieves the best speed-accuracy trade-off on the MS COCO dataset, with 28.1% AP at 142 FPS, 37.4% AP at 52 FPS, and 45.1% AP with multi-scale testing at 1.4 FPS.
Hourglass-104 achieves the best accuracy at a relatively good speed, with a 42.2% AP in 7.8 FPS.
DLA-34 gives the best speed/accuracy trade-off. It runs at 52FPS with 37.4%AP.

limitations.summary: The center representation can only fire once per shared center, direct keypoint regression for pose is not state-of-the-art without joint-detection matching, and an attempted multi-anchor extension of CenterNet failed.
items: Two perfectly aligned objects that share a center point yield only one detection (the authors measure this at under 0.1% of COCO objects).
Direct regression of human keypoints struggles particularly in high IoU regimes and trails state-of-the-art pose estimators.
A multiple-anchor version of CenterNet regressing to more than one object size did not succeed.

evidence.quote: In unlucky circumstances, two different objects might share the same center, if they perfectly align. In this scenario, CenterNet would only detect one of them.
Direct regression to keypoints performs reasonably, but not at state-of-the-art. It struggles particularly in high IoU regimes.
Finally, we tried a multiple “anchor” version of CenterNet by regressing to more than one object size. The experiments did not yield any success.

equations.expr: L_k = -(1/N) * sum over xyc of alpha*(1-Y_hat)*log(Y_hat) if Y=1 else (1-Y)^beta*Y_hat^alpha*log(1-Y_hat)

evidence.quote: Our method performs competitively with sophisticated multi-stage methods and runs in real-time.
The running time is tested on our local machine, with Intel Core i7-8086K CPU, Titan Xp GPU, Pytorch 0.4.1, CUDA 9.0, and CUDNN 7.1.
